title: Let LLMs Wander: Engineering RL Environments — Stefano Fiorucci

primary.label: Post-Training & Continual Learning
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 90%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's core focus is adapting models after pretraining via SFT warm-up and RL with verifiable rewards using GRPO/CISPO, fitting post-training and continual learning. The content demonstrates general-purpose RL environment engineering and training methodology not tied to a specific application vertical. The talk covers both training (SFT, RL with CISPO) and evaluation (programmatic evals, rollout inspection, live gameplay) stages. Requires familiarity with RL concepts, LLM training phases, and Python programming, but provides introductory framing of classic RL before advancing. Structured as a practical tutorial walking through environment construction, training pipeline execution, and iterative improvement with code demonstrations. Multiple grounded evidence anchors from the transcript directly support the classification with specific quantitative claims and demonstrations.

summary: Stefano Fiorucci presents on engineering RL environments for LLMs, beginning with classic RL concepts—agent, environment, state, action, reward, trajectory—and mapping them to the language model domain. He reviews the standard three-phase LLM training recipe and motivates the shift toward RL with verifiable rewards, citing DeepSeek R1's GRPO and OpenAI O1's compute scaling. Unlike SFT, RL lets models explore trajectories and discover reasoning strategies beyond human data quality. He introduces Verifiers by Prime Intellect, providing modular base classes for single-turn, multi-turn, and tool environments, with integrations to training frameworks. Concrete examples include a reverse-text single-turn environment and a double-check multi-turn environment. Tool environments extend multi-turn foundations with Python function tools, MCP server connectivity, and stateful tools for per-rollout persistence. The core case study is tic-tac-toe: a simple game requiring multi-turn interaction that small models struggle with. The environment is built iteratively—starting with a basic version where the model plays X, outputs moves in XML tags, and faces a random opponent. Improvements include alternating play order, a minimax optimal opponent with controllable randomness, reasoning traces via think tags, invalid move penalties instead of immediate losses, and noise reduction through seeded opponents and stratified sampling across batches. Evaluation reveals GPT-5 mini plays well while LFM-2 by Liquid AI struggles with format and valid moves. A warm-up SFT phase using 200 synthetic games generated by GPT-5 mini teaches format and valid move syntax. RL training with CISPO uses stratified sampling, opponent difficulty ranging 20-70% random, and careful batch size tuning to avoid model collapse. Results show LFM-2 becoming a competent player—dominating random opponents and drawing 85% against optimal ones, with invalid moves near zero. A final iteration increases opponent skill to 0-25% random and uses temperature tuning to encourage exploration beyond memorized strategies, producing an initial reward drop followed by recovery to new highs. The trained model outperforms GPT-5 mini against optimal opponents. Stefano shares lessons from failed experiments: large batch sizes yield stable but slow training while small ones risk collapse; hidden biases in minimax opponents can cause memorization rather than genuine learning; reasoning-pre-trained models may waste GPU budget on long traces; very small models can be hard to push to competency; and practitioners should inspect rollouts, play against the model beyond programmatic evaluation, and avoid prematurely stopping training runs. He concludes that RL with verifiable rewards complements SFT in post-training and is accessible to practitioners with limited resources, recommending his free LLM RL environments course and the environments hub as next steps.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Classic RL concepts map directly to LLMs: the model is the agent, the environment provides data, harnesses, and scoring rules.
RL with verifiable rewards enables models to explore trajectories and discover strategies beyond human example quality, unlike SFT imitation.
Verifiers by Prime Intellect provides modular environment classes, tool environments with MCP integration, and the environments hub to fight fragmentation in open-source RL.
Iterative environment engineering is essential: start simple, verify with evaluation, then add realistic features like controllable opponent skill, reasoning traces, and noise reduction.
Reducing environment noise is critical for GRPO-based training: seeded opponents ensure fair rollout comparison, and stratified sampling balances opponent difficulty across batches.
A warm-up SFT phase with synthetic data teaches format and valid moves before RL builds deeper capabilities, illustrating a practical two-stage training approach.
RL training is sensitive to hyperparameters—especially batch size—where too-small batches cause model collapse and suboptimal strategies.
Hidden biases in environments can cause memorization rather than genuine learning; practitioners must inspect rollouts and play against the model beyond programmatic evaluation.
Temperature tuning can encourage exploration beyond memorized strategies, with an initial reward drop signaling an exploratory phase before recovery.

RL with verifiable rewards complements SFT in post-training and is accessible to practitioners with limited GPU resources for building specialized small models that beat large closed models on specific tasks.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.summary: Stefano introduces himself as an AI/SW engineer at Deepset working on Haystack, and motivates RL environments for LLMs by citing DeepSeek and MiniMax using thousands of environments, with startups getting major funding.

sections.title: Classic RL Refresher
sections.summary: Reviews core RL concepts: agent, environment, state, action, reward, trajectory/rollout, exploration vs exploitation, and cumulative reward maximization.

sections.title: LLM Training and Shift to RL
sections.summary: Covers the three-phase LLM training recipe (pre-training, SFT, RL alignment), cites Sutskever on pre-training limits, OpenAI O1 on RL and compute scaling, and DeepSeek R1 on GRPO and RL with verifiable rewards as an alternative to expensive SFT data.

sections.title: Mapping RL to LLMs and Tic-Tac-Toe Example
sections.summary: Maps RL concepts to LLMs: model as agent, environment as game engine with data/harnesses/scoring rules, actions as text responses, rewards guiding strategy discovery. Tic-tac-toe used as concrete example. Cites Karpathy on interaction enabling more than statistical expert imitation.

sections.title: Verifiers Library Overview
sections.summary: Introduces Verifiers by Prime Intellect: modular Python packages for RL environments, base classes for single-turn/multi-turn/tool setups, abstractions for parsing and reward functions, OpenAI-compatible API serving, parallel trajectory handling, and training integrations with Prime RL, Tinker, Sky RL.

sections.title: Single-Turn Environment: Reverse Text
sections.summary: Demonstrates reverse text environment: dataset loading and mapping, XML parser initialization, reward function via longest common subsequence, rubric creation, and evaluation run with 5 examples × 3 rollouts = 15 total rollouts.

sections.title: Multi-Turn and Tool Environments
sections.summary: Covers double-check multi-turn environment (state tracking, environment responses like 'Are you sure?', stop-condition decorator) and introduces tool environments as built on multi-turn foundations.

sections.title: Advanced Tool Environments and Environments Hub
sections.summary: Details tool environment mechanics: Python function tools, model calls tools during rollouts and receives results. Introduces NCP environment for MCP servers, stateful tool environment for per-rollout persistence, recursive language models for unbounded context. Covers environments hub for sharing RL environments and fighting fragmentation.

sections.title: Tic-Tac-Toe Environment: Basic Version
sections.summary: Motivates tic-tac-toe as simple but challenging for small models. Basic version: model plays X and goes first, outputs 0-8 in move tags, random opponent. Covers load environment, setup state with board/winner, response with game logic, winner reward (weight 1) and format reward (weight 0.2).

sections.title: Tic-Tac-Toe Environment: Iterative Improvements
sections.summary: Improves environment: alternating play order, minimax optimal opponent with controllable random move probability, think tags for reasoning, invalid move penalty of -0.1 instead of immediate loss, seeded opponents for GRPO noise reduction, stratified sampling for balanced opponent difficulty across batches.

sections.title: Model Evaluation and SFT Warm-Up
sections.summary: Evaluates GPT-5 mini (excellent format, good player) and LFM-2 by Liquid AI (struggles with format and valid moves). Generates 200 synthetic games with GPT-5 mini for SFT warm-up, filters losses, runs SFT with Prime RL on 96GB GPU in minutes. Post-SFT model learns format and reduces invalid moves.

sections.title: RL Training with CISPO and Results
sections.summary: Recaps GRPO applied to tic-tac-toe: rollouts from same board, deterministic rewards, advantage computation. Uses CISPO (improvement over GRPO). Training config: 20-70% random opponent, stratified sampling, batch size below 256 to avoid collapse. Results: model dominates random players, draws 85% vs optimal, invalid moves near zero.

sections.title: Advanced Iteration: Pushing Toward Perfection
sections.summary: Identifies fork trap failure modes in trained model. Increases opponent skill to 0-25% random. Notes that pure optimal opponents made model overly defensive. Explores how to make model explore beyond learned strategies.

sections.title: Temperature Tuning, Final Results, and Live Game
sections.summary: Uses temperature to encourage exploration beyond memorized strategies. Training shows initial reward drop (exploratory phase) followed by recovery to new highs. Format and invalid move rewards remain near maximum. Final evaluation confirms tic-tac-toe mastery. Live game played against model demonstrates competent blocking and winning. Trained LFM-2 compared to GPT-5 mini teacher: similar vs random, superior vs optimal opponent.

sections.title: Lessons from Failed Experiments
sections.summary: Shares practical lessons: large batch sizes give stable but slow training; small batch sizes with diverse environments risk reinforcing suboptimal strategies and collapse. Hidden biases in minimax (always selecting first free position among equal moves) caused memorization rather than generalization. Reasoning-pre-trained models waste GPU budget on long traces; better to start from base model. Very small models hard to push to competency—evaluate base models and choose promising ones. Inspect rollouts, play against model beyond programmatic evaluation. Watch logs early for OOM/instability, then let training run without premature tweaking.

sections.title: Conclusion and Resources
sections.summary: Recaps the journey: mapping RL to LLMs, Verifiers library, tic-tac-toe experiments with SFT and RL. Emphasizes RL complements SFT in post-training and is accessible at home with limited resources. Recommends free LLM RL environments course, environments hub, and training small models on 2-3 tools to outperform large models on specific tasks. Suggests Wiki search example in Prime RL as starting point.
